title: What not to put on the site for a fintech product
metaTitle: Fintech product website mistakes to cut
excerpt: Cut abstract trust language from a fintech site. Keep the product, the people responsible, and a clear way to open an account or talk to sales.
alt: Three pale speckled bottles on a gray surface, two holding dried seed heads, a small set of objects for a page about what to leave off a site.
caption: Three bottles, two of them holding dried stems. A shorter shelf is easier to trust. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the most common mistake on a fintech website?
faqs.answer: Leading with abstract trust language instead of the product and the people responsible. Lines about being safe, seamless, or bank-grade reassure the team and give a buyer nothing to check. Replace them with the product state, the entity or partner, and a way to start an account or talk to sales.

faqs.question: Should a fintech site publish every policy in the navigation?
faqs.answer: Publish the policies a buyer may need, and link them with plain names from the footer and from the claim they support. Do not turn the header into a library of PDFs. A license, a funds note, and a privacy page are easier to find when the main nav is reserved for the product, the price, and the path.

faqs.question: Is a longer site more credible for a money product?
faqs.answer: No. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long one that performs taste. Extra pages of manifesto, unnamed logos, and feature dumps make the accountable facts harder to find. Add a page when a real question needs room, not when the homepage feels bare.

markdown:
The fintech product website mistakes that cost you a careful buyer are usually additions. Abstract trust language reassures the team and confuses someone who may hand you money. Cut it.

Keep the product, the people responsible, and a clear way to start an account or talk to sales. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long one that performs taste.

## Cut abstract trust language

Start with the sentences that sound like every other money brand. "Your funds are safe with us." "Built on trust." "Security is in our DNA." "Seamless infrastructure for the future of finance." None of these show a payout, a hold, or a person. They occupy the first screen, which is the only screen some buyers will give you.

Google's helpful-content guidance is direct about the failure mode. People-first pages help a visitor finish a job. Search-engine-first pages, and by the same logic slogan-first pages, leave people feeling they must look elsewhere for the real information. On a topic that can affect someone's financial stability, Google also says trust carries extra weight. A slogan is not a trust signal. A checkable fact is.

Replace the line, do not decorate it. "We do not hold customer funds. Partner Bank N.A. does, and here is the license note" is a replacement if it is true. "Exceptions over this threshold are reviewed by a person" is a replacement if it is true. If you cannot say the fact yet, say the product and the path, and leave the adjective out. Absence of a fake sentence is better than presence of one.

Do the same to buttons and nav labels. "Get started" is abstract. "Open an account" is a job. "Learn more" is abstract. The name of the page they will open is a job. The cut list includes every control whose label could be swapped onto another company without edit.

## Cut the trophy wall

Unnamed logos, award badges, and "as seen in" strips are the visual version of abstract trust. They ask the buyer to feel impressed instead of informed. A logo with a sentence about the constraint can stay, on a proof page. A row of marks with no sentence should come off the homepage, where it pushes the path down the screen.

Awards and headcount belong on the cut list unless the number changes the decision. "Forty people" does not tell a buyer who reviews a failed payout. A named role does. Press logos do not tell them whether you serve their country. The pricing page does. Put the energy into the page that answers the question they brought.

Investor logos follow the same rule. Publish them if a serious buyer expects the cap table signal and you can say it accurately. Do not let them become the hero. The hero is the product. A homepage that leads with other people's brands is a homepage that does not yet believe its own screen.

Customer quotes need a name, a role, and a fact, and you need permission. A quote you cannot attribute, about a result you cannot explain, is a trophy. Cut it. A short story with a constraint and a decision can live on a proof page. It does not need to be repeated in a carousel on every template.

## Cut the feature dump

A grid of twenty capabilities is how a product team avoids choosing a buyer. Each cell is true and none of them help. The buyer wanted to know if seller payouts in two countries are the job you do. They got "ledgering," "orchestration," "risk," "analytics," and "APIs" in matching cards.

Keep the jobs. Link each job to a service block with an outcome and a boundary. Move API detail to the docs, where a builder will look for it. Move internal architecture to a conversation, unless a technical buyer cannot trust you without a specific diagram. Even then, one diagram with a caption beats twelve icons.

Cut pages that restate the homepage for a synonym. A "platform" page, a "product" page, and a "solutions" page that share the same six claims are one page pretending to be three. Google's warning about producing lots of pages in the hope some of them rank is the content version of this habit. Merge them. Redirect the extras. Give the survivor one title that says what it is.

Also cut the glossary you wrote for yourselves. If a term needs a definition the buyer did not ask for, you are teaching your vocabulary instead of doing their job. Use their word in the heading. Define your word once, in a subordinate clause, if a returning customer searches for it.

## Cut pages that only perform seriousness

Some pages exist so the site feels regulated, funded, or grown-up. A culture page of posters. A newsroom with two posts. A 40-page PDF of a brand story linked from the header. A "trust center" that is a lock icon and three adjectives. These pages reassure internal reviewers. They dilute the facts a buyer came to check.

Keep the serious pages that answer a real question. Security practices you actually follow. The license. The privacy note. The subprocessors, if you publish them. The status of funds. Write those in plain sentences and link them from the claim they support. Do not bundle them under a mood called Trust and then neglect the words.

Cut countdown timers, fake scarcity, and "limited onboarding slots" unless a real capacity constraint exists and you are willing to honor it. Urgency on a money form feels like pressure. Pressure is the opposite of the tone a careful buyer is testing you for. A calm page that says "we onboard a set number of new entities a month, and here is how the queue works" is allowed because it is operational. A red banner is not.

Cut chat widgets that cover the account button and open with "How can I help you today?" before the buyer has read what you do. If you have a staffed support chat for customers, load it after login. The marketing site can offer the named paths without a bubble.

## Cut motion and decoration that delay the product

Autoplay video, parallax skylines, and cursor effects are often the last holdouts of a brand exercise. They delay the product image and they move the layout while the buyer is trying to tap. On a phone, which is where this decision usually happens, they are the difference between seeing the payout and seeing a loader.

Hanabi's own bar is that a marketing site should be fast before it is clever, built in Next.js with Tailwind, and animated with Motion only when the motion explains something. Reduced motion is part of done. A fintech homepage does not need a three-second intro to earn the right to show a ledger. The ledger is the intro.

Cut stock photographs of handshakes, cash, and glass towers. They are decoration pretending to be evidence. Use the product and the people, or use type. A well-set sentence is more credible than a rented skyline. Photography direction is a cut list as much as a shot list.

Cut duplicate footers full of keyword links. If the header is doing its job, the footer can repeat the jobs once and then list the legal pages. A second sitemap written for robots is a page-weight you do not need, and it is a sign the primary pages are not clear enough to stand alone.

## A cut list you can run this week

Take the homepage, the nav, and the contact page. Mark every block with one of three notes. Proves the product. Names a person or an entity. Starts an account or a sales conversation. Anything without a note is a candidate to remove.

A practical order:

1. Delete the abstract headline. Write the job and the buyer.
2. Remove logo rows that have no story.
3. Collapse synonym pages into one URL.
4. Take feature grids down to the jobs you want to be hired for.
5. Unstick every widget that covers the action.
6. Read the first phone screen out loud.

Then read what remains to someone outside the company. If they can say what you do, who is responsible, and what they would tap, the site is shorter and more credible. If they cannot, you cut the wrong thing. Put back a fact, not a slogan.

Keep a record of what you removed and why, so the next redesign does not restore the skyline out of habit. On a Hanabi project those notes live in the client portal with the brand files and the page docs. The public site stays small. The reason it is small stays findable.

When you want help deciding what to cut before you redraw the rest, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the current homepage. The useful outcome is a shorter page, not a longer sitemap.

## What a short site still owes the buyer

Short does not mean missing. The price shape, the boundary of the service, the funds fact, and the response time on the contact path are not decoration. They are the content. A one-page site that includes them can be enough. A ten-page site that avoids them is the mistake this piece is about.

Do not cut the accessible name of a button, the text alternative of a product image, or the error on a form in the name of minimalism. Those are the page. Minimalism is fewer claims. It is not less clarity.

Review the site every time the product changes a boundary. A page you were proud to shorten can grow a new slogan in a single campaign. The cut list is a habit, not a launch task. The buyer who shows up next month deserves the same plain page as the buyer who showed up the week you edited it.

If the next site you are editing is a clinic rather than a money product, the mistake changes shape. Stock smiles and a procedure menu replace the trust slogans, and the buyer is anxious rather than cautious. [What the homepage has to prove for a small clinic](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-small-clinic) starts that decision from the other side of the waiting room.
